lead: Corrosion eats steel where an electrolyte, usually oxygen, and an anodic site meet. Some soils and closed systems corrode even with little oxygen. Control means breaking that electrochemical cell. One way is cathodic protection: supply electrons so the steel becomes the cathode and stops dissolving. Another is a protective coating: a barrier keeps water and oxygen away from the surface. A third is an inhibitor: a chemical that slows the electrode reactions. These methods are used on buried pipelines, ship hulls, water tanks, bridge rebars and car bodies. This chapter explains the methods, their limits and the design rules that make them work.
prereq: You need: 4.8 for the corrosion cell and galvanic series, and the electrode reactions in 4.1 and 4.2.

sections.h3: Cathodic protection: two ways to supply electrons

blocks.text: At an anodic site, metal dissolves: M → Mⁿ⁺ + n e⁻. Here M is the metal atom and n is the number of electrons. At the cathode, oxygen or hydrogen ions accept electrons. Cathodic protection makes the whole steel surface the cathode. An external source supplies the electrons that the anodic reaction would otherwise release. The steel potential shifts negative and dissolution stops.

Sacrificial anode. Connect the steel to a metal that is more active in the galvanic series, such as zinc, magnesium or an aluminium alloy. This anode corrodes in place of the steel. The steel is the cathode. The method needs no power supply and suits buried pipelines, water tanks and ship hulls. The anode is consumed and must be replaced.

Impressed current. Use a DC supply. Connect its positive terminal to an inert anode, such as graphite or mixed metal oxide, and its negative terminal to the steel. The anode sits in the electrolyte, soil or water. The supply pushes current from the anode through the electrolyte to the steel. The steel becomes the cathode. This method suits large structures and high-resistivity soil. The current can be adjusted.

The protection potential for buried steel is about −0.85 V against a copper-copper sulfate reference electrode. A second criterion is a negative shift of 100 mV from the natural potential. The current needed depends on area, coating quality and soil resistivity:

blocks.where: I is the total protection current in amperes (A); i is the required current density in amperes per square metre (A m⁻²); A is the protected area in square metres (m²). If i is in mA m⁻², I comes out in mA.

blocks.text: Too much current is overprotection. It produces hydrogen at the steel, can disbond coatings and can embrittle high-strength steel. Set the current by potential measurement, not by guess.

sections.h3: Coatings: paint, metal and oxide layers

blocks.text: Coatings block the electrolyte or change the surface chemistry. Good surface preparation matters more than thick paint. A paint has a pigment, a binder and a solvent. The binder forms the film; the pigment gives colour and can inhibit corrosion. Varnish is a clear resin coating. Enamel is a hard, often heat-cured coating.

items: Galvanizing dips steel in molten zinc or electrodeposits zinc. Zinc is anodic to steel. A scratch exposes steel, but the nearby zinc corrodes first and protects the steel. This is sacrificial protection.

Tinning coats steel with tin. Tin is cathodic to steel. A scratch exposes steel and tin. The small exposed steel area becomes the anode and the large tin area the cathode. The anode current density is high and the steel pits rapidly. Tinplate food cans need a lacquer.

Electroplating deposits a metal such as nickel, chromium or zinc from a solution using current. It gives a decorative or hard layer. A thin plating with pores can make corrosion worse if the plated metal is cathodic to the base.
Anodizing makes aluminium the anode in an electrolyte, so a thick aluminium oxide layer grows. The layer is hard and can be dyed.

blocks.text: Conversion coatings change the metal surface into a phosphate or chromate layer. They improve paint adhesion. A multilayer coating combines a primer, an intermediate coat and a topcoat. The primer bonds and inhibits, the intermediate coat gives barrier thickness, and the topcoat resists weather and abrasion. Each layer has a job; one thick layer is not the same.

Inhibitors are chemicals added in small amounts to water, acid or a closed system. An anodic inhibitor forms a passive oxide film on the anode, for example nitrite, molybdate or chromate. If the dose is too low, it covers only part of the surface and pitting can become worse. A cathodic inhibitor slows the cathodic reaction, often by precipitating a film at cathodic sites. A mixed inhibitor adsorbs on both sites; many organic amines work this way. Inhibitors are common in cooling water, boiler water, pickling acids and closed loops.
Design rules reduce the chance of a corrosion cell:

items: Avoid dissimilar metal joints. If they are unavoidable, insulate them and keep the less noble metal large compared with the noble one.
Drain moisture. Shape the part so water runs off and cannot collect in crevices.
Avoid crevices and trapped water under washers, gaskets and coatings.
Use inhibitors where the same water is recirculated.
Maintain coatings. A small break in a barrier coating can become a small anode beside a large cathode.
Design for inspection and replacement of anodes.

blocks.text: Cathodic protection and coatings work together. A coating lowers the current needed; cathodic protection covers the breaks. Do not use a coating that disbonds under cathodic protection. Check the protection potential after installation and at intervals.

figure.caption: The tree groups corrosion control into cathodic protection and coatings. Both cathodic branches make the steel the cathode while a separate anode corrodes or passes current.

spec.aria: A corrosion-control tree splits into cathodic protection by sacrificial anode or impressed current, and coatings such as paint and zinc coating.

examples.question: A steel water tank has a wetted area of 20 m². The coating is in poor condition, and the required protection current density is 10 mA m⁻². Find the total protection current in mA and in A.
steps: Use I = i × A = 10 mA m⁻² × 20 m² = 200 mA.
The current is 200 mA or 0.20 A.
examples.answer: The total protection current is 200 mA, which is 0.20 A.
examples.check:
i = 10  # mA per m^2
A = 20  # m^2
I_mA = i * A
I_A = I_mA / 1000
print(I_mA)
print(I_A)

traps: In cathodic protection the protected steel is the cathode. The sacrificial anode is the metal that corrodes. Reversing these two loses marks.
Overprotection is not extra safety. Too negative a potential evolves hydrogen, disbonds coatings and can crack high-strength steel.

Galvanizing and tinning are not the same. Zinc is anodic to steel and protects a scratch; tin is cathodic, so a scratch in tinplate leaves a small steel anode beside a large tin cathode and the exposed steel corrodes fast.
A low dose of an anodic inhibitor can worsen pitting. The inhibitor must cover the whole surface.
Keep current-density units consistent. mA m⁻² × m² gives mA; divide by 1000 for A. Do not mix cm² with m².

quiz.q: Name the two types of cathodic protection.
Why does making steel the cathode stop corrosion?
quiz.a: The anodic dissolution reaction needs the metal to be the anode. When electrons are supplied, the steel potential shifts negative, the steel becomes the cathode, and oxidation of iron stops.

quiz.q: A buried pipe of area 12 m² needs 8 mA m⁻². Find the protection current.
A galvanized steel sheet and a tinplate sheet are scratched to bare steel. Which resists rust better at the scratch? Explain.
quiz.a: The galvanized sheet. Zinc is anodic to steel and corrodes first, protecting the exposed steel. Tin is cathodic to steel, so at the scratch the small exposed steel area acts as the anode against the large tin cathode, and the steel corrodes faster.

quiz.q: What is an anodic inhibitor? Give one example.
quiz.a: A chemical that forms a passive oxide film on the anode and slows metal dissolution; nitrite, molybdate or chromate.

quiz.q: Why should a design avoid dissimilar metal joints?
quiz.a: They form a galvanic cell. The less noble metal becomes the anode and corrodes faster, especially if its area is small compared with the noble metal.

quiz.q: Why is a pinhole in a paint film dangerous?
quiz.a: The pinhole exposes a small anode while the surrounding coated area acts as a large cathode. The small anode has a high current density, so pitting can be rapid.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern pipeline operators use remote monitoring and solar-powered impressed-current units, and they combine potential readings with coating surveys. Offshore wind foundations and reinforced-concrete bridges use cathodic protection with reference electrodes cast into the structure. Newer coatings include graphene-enhanced barrier films and chromate-free conversion layers. Search for impressed current cathodic protection, sacrificial anode design, coating disbondment and corrosion inhibitors.
